curation.scope: Bay Area storefront and institutional exterior qualitative reference library
curation.dimensions: All profile geometry ranges are explicit inference priors, not measured facts or legal requirements.
curation.photo_policy: Reference URLs and original observations only; third-party project photographs and plan sheets are not redistributed.
curation.replica_policy: Only unchanged supplied brand assets or caller-observed facade components may be exact; generic chain shells are never labeled replicas.

sources.title: Formula Retail Storefront Design
sources.locator: Storefront Components and Formula Retail Storefront Design
observations: Storefront bays distinguish piers, bulkheads, glazing, transoms and entrances.
Retain historic components when inserting chain identity; a brand does not imply a replacement building shell.

sources.title: Downtown Historic Design Standards
observations: Awnings fit between piers and should leave transoms visible.
Sloped awnings and signs belong to individual storefront bays, not across unrelated tenants.

sources.title: Standards for Storefront Transparency
observations: Front display glazing remains visually open rather than fully covered by invented posters.
The guidance concerns storefront visibility, not a measurement of any existing store.

sources.title: Calle 24 Special Area Design Guidelines
observations: Neighborhood signs include awnings, painted signs and multilingual business identity.
Laundromat examples combine an overhead identity band and limited window lettering.

sources.title: Starbucks Creative Expression: Logos and Color
observations: The Siren and wordmark are distinct brand elements.
Greens, neutrals and a restrained type system provide recognizable identity.
This reference is a visual identity guide, not a universal exterior elevation.

sources.title: Starbucks Bay Area projects
sources.location: San Francisco Chestnut, Mission & Main, Market
sources.locator: Mission & Main exterior photograph; visually inspected
observations: Mission & Main photograph: tall black-framed glazing with transom, a deep soffit and gold-toned illuminated lettering.
Reserve locations and standard coffeehouses have different expressions.
Existing structure and local conditions drive individual site detailing.

sources.title: Starbucks Store Design
observations: Designs respond to neighborhood character and use local materials.
Do not assert that every Starbucks has the same facade.

sources.title: Subway visual identity
observations: Arrow-ended logotype and yellow/green identity were developed as a coordinated system.
Signage is part of a wider environmental identity; the type is custom.

sources.title: Subway Unveils New Global Restaurant Design
sources.locator: Exterior media item 19669; visually inspected, a design rendering not a built-site survey
observations: Published exterior concept has a green fascia with yellow/white dimensional wordmark, white cladding and a glass front with green-framed entry.
Front glazing and solid side wall have different functions.
Fresh Forward 2.0 rollout does not establish the remodel status of a particular Bay Area store.

sources.title: Subway Fresh Forward signage
observations: Signage was prototyped and value-engineered as a repeatable franchise system.

sources.title: Safeway Shopping Center 180 El Camino Real
sources.locator: Approved Project Plans, cover rendering visually inspected; October 2017 approval
observations: Customer-facing elevation combines broad glass storefront bays with brick and plaster framing.
Loading and back-of-house side/rear walls are different from the public front.
Approved plan shows dark lettering and a red S medallion; it does not prove the present-day as-built condition.

sources.title: Safeway sign specifications, Oakley
sources.locator: SAFEWAY SIGN SPECIFICATIONS; indexed text, dimensions not transcribed
observations: Sign specification calls for LED channel letters/logo and maintaining letter height-to-width ratios.
Sign size is site dependent, not a fixed fraction of every Safeway.

sources.title: Whole Foods Market Oakland
observations: Historic facade is retained in an adaptive reuse.
A steel and glass connection links the store with rooftop and street-level parking.
This facade cannot be copied as a standard suburban Whole Foods shell.

sources.title: Whole Foods Market national program
observations: Exterior design is coordinated with developers and location-specific goals.
Neighborhood context varies across the chain.

sources.title: Trader Joes market program
observations: Work covers many existing and new market shells, including exterior elevations.
Practical adaptation and city requirements differ by location.

sources.title: Trader Joes Signage
observations: Brand lettering coexists with local illustrated and hand-made sign treatments.
Do not replace every location with an identical architectural shell.

sources.title: Peets 2078–2080 Chestnut Street
sources.locator: 2013 packet p36, sheet A3.1; visually inspected
observations: Proposed elevation retains a historic entry, tile base and upper decorative facade.
New glazing aligns with existing glazing; signs avoid historic tile.
Street-level transparency is documented as 72.6 percent for this proposal, not a chain-wide ratio.

sources.title: Peets Coffee prototype program
observations: Prototype kit balances wood, stone, tile and metal.
Drive-through and walk-in formats differ and retain site-specific adaptation.

sources.title: Designing the Community Coffee House
observations: A large finish catalogue is used to keep individual stores distinct.
Local graphics and site-specific colors sit within a consistent coffeehouse identity.

sources.title: 7-Eleven Brand Identity
sources.locator: Store.jpg on the original designer portfolio; visually inspected
observations: Three colored stripes remain an important identity device.
The identity update is not evidence for a store-specific remodel.
The published storefront example has orange above green above red, interrupted by centered identity on a white fascia over brick and glass.

sources.title: 7-Eleven Media Kit
observations: Official brand graphics and store imagery provide reference for logo/stripe identity.

sources.title: Chipotle Eco Concept Pilot
observations: Wood and metal form a restrained repeatable kit of parts.
Pickup-focused and dine-in flows can use different shells; atmosphere is not excessive signage.

sources.title: Chipotle rollout projects
observations: Prototype components are tailored to each site rather than changing the brand identity.

sources.title: JPMorgan Chase Savannah
observations: Historic storefront and entry details are retained rather than replaced with a generic bank box.

sources.title: Bank and Financial Institution Signage
observations: Channel letters, logos, wayfinding and ATM identity are distinct sign components.

sources.title: CVS 701 Portola Drive elevations
sources.locator: CVS 1983, sheet A-3; indexed text, historical proposal
observations: The plan differentiates clear customer glazing from stockroom walls.
A metal canopy and cornice articulate a corner retail facade.

sources.title: Walgreens Los Angeles elevations
observations: Pharmacy identity and window arrangements vary by elevation and existing structure.
Legacy operating-hour and photo-service claims are not reused as current advertisements.

sources.title: Anchor Oyster Bar Legacy Business
observations: The small restaurant has a broad plate-glass window and a blue awning.
A narrow business can be recognizable without a large plastic fascia.

sources.title: Bix Restaurant
observations: A discreet alley entrance and a characteristic neon sign identify an upscale restaurant.
High price does not automatically imply huge windows or oversized signage.

sources.title: Gino and Carlo
observations: A distinctive projecting neon blade sign identifies the bar.

sources.title: Little Joes Pizza
observations: Historic neon identity is a meaningful pizza-shop variant, not a universal requirement.

sources.title: Great Wall Hardware
observations: Exterior includes bilingual business identification and a practical overhead sign.

sources.title: William Stout Architectural Books
observations: A historic storefront provides the setting for a specialist bookstore.
Display identity should leave the building architecture legible.

sources.title: Credo Beauty flagship
observations: Expansive operable glazing and a generous entry alcove connect the store to the street.
Textured neutral plaster is punctuated by the brand color.

sources.title: Rossi and Rovetti Flower Shop
observations: Contemporary flower display and flexible retail bins distinguish the flower-shop program.

sources.title: La Mar
observations: A glass canopy and large entrance identity are inserted within a historic pier facade.
Restaurant context can change sign scale more than cuisine does.

sources.title: Brucato Amaro
observations: Restaurant entry and shipping/receiving are adjacent but perform different roles.
Tiled materials and neon/vertical identity are shown in project documentation.

sources.title: Belmont Village Albany
observations: Senior living is a multi-storey residential/institutional envelope with a distinct common entrance.
Ground parking and upper residential windows must not be converted into storefront display glass.

sources.title: Belmont Village signage program
observations: Identity letters, plaques, directories, addresses and wayfinding form a coordinated campus sign system.
Advertising across every window is not the institutional program.

sources.title: Forest Avenue Medical Center wayfinding
observations: Multi-tenant medical uses need a shared directory and entrance/wayfinding identity.
A directory is different from individual shop advertisements.

sources.title: Office, Business Park, Institutional and Industrial Design
observations: Signage is coordinated with architecture and landscaping.
Office and institutional identity is organized at entrances rather than repeated storefront advertisements.

sources.title: Coffee shop design practice
observations: Brand and environmental graphics are separate from the shell.
Existing chain spaces can be reused with different independent cafe identities.

sources.title: Mels Drive-In history and exterior documentation
sources.locator: Historic restaurant photographs and neon identity
observations: Merchant photographs document the drive-in diner tradition, broad customer glazing and neon identity.
Historic and current-format examples are not a universal contemporary diner elevation.
